title: TCP Congestion Control
summary: Specifies the four congestion control algorithms TCP uses to avoid overwhelming the network: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit, and fast recovery. It also covers how to resume sending after an idle period and some guidance on generating acknowledgments. It is a Draft Standard on the standards track.

eli5.summary: If everyone pours water into a pipe too fast, it overflows. TCP starts with a trickle, speeds up while things go well, and slows down when it notices trouble, so the shared pipe does not clog.

subtitle: The rules that make TCP start gently, grow carefully and back off when the network shows signs of overload.

tldr.problem: If every TCP sender transmitted as fast as it could, the shared network would be overloaded, and the senders would not know how much capacity is available.
tldr.mechanism: A sender keeps a congestion window (cwnd) limiting how much data it has in flight, grows it with slow start and congestion avoidance, and cuts it back when loss is detected, using fast retransmit and fast recovery to repair single losses quickly.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5681 obsoletes RFC 2581 and is a Draft Standard. It has since been updated by RFC 9438, and it relies on correct implementation to avoid congestion collapse.

today: RFC 5681 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 2581 and has been updated by RFC 9438.

sections.title: Four Algorithms for Sharing the Network
sections.content:
RFC 5681 specifies four TCP congestion control algorithms: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery. They were devised by Van Jacobson in 1988 and 1990 and are standardized for use with TCP in RFC 1122. The base protocol is RFC 793.

The document also says what a TCP connection should do after a long idle period and clarifies how acknowledgments should be generated. It obsoletes RFC 2581, which in turn obsoleted RFC 2001.

The algorithms treat loss as the signal of congestion. Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) could also be used, as specified in RFC 3168.
sections.eli5: TCP has four rules for being a polite driver on a busy road: start slowly, speed up carefully, slow down when there is a jam, and recover quickly after a bump.

sections.title: Key Terms and Variables
sections.content:
The congestion window (cwnd) is a sender-side limit on the data it can send. The receiver window (rwnd) is the most recently advertised window. A TCP MUST NOT send data with a sequence number higher than the highest acknowledged sequence number plus the minimum of cwnd and rwnd.

Sizes are measured in terms of the sender maximum segment size (SMSS) and the receiver maximum segment size (RMSS). If the receiver sends no MSS option, RMSS is 536 bytes. Flight size is the data sent but not yet cumulatively acknowledged.

Three special window values are named: the initial window (IW) after the three-way handshake, the loss window (LW) after a retransmission timeout, and the restart window (RW) after an idle period.

A duplicate acknowledgment has five conditions: the receiver of the ACK has outstanding data, the ACK carries no data, the SYN and FIN bits are off, its acknowledgment number equals the greatest received on the connection, and its advertised window equals that of the last ACK. A SACK-capable TCP may use SACK information instead.
sections.eli5: TCP keeps two numbers for how much it may send: one for what the network can take and one for what the other side can take. It always obeys the smaller one.

sections.title: Slow Start and Congestion Avoidance
sections.content:
Slow start and congestion avoidance MUST be used by a TCP sender. A third variable, the slow start threshold (ssthresh), decides which one applies: slow start when cwnd < ssthresh, congestion avoidance when cwnd > ssthresh, and either when they are equal. The initial ssthresh SHOULD be arbitrarily high, but it MUST be reduced in response to congestion.

The initial window depends on SMSS: at most 4 segments for SMSS up to 1095 bytes, 3 segments above that up to 2190, and 2 segments above 2190. If the SYN or SYN/ACK is lost, the initial window is one segment of at most SMSS bytes.

In slow start, cwnd grows by at most SMSS for each ACK that covers new data. The RFC recommends cwnd += min (N, SMSS), where N is the number of newly acknowledged bytes. This Appropriate Byte Counting defends against ACK Division, where a receiver sends several ACKs for one segment to inflate the window.

In congestion avoidance, cwnd grows by roughly one full-sized segment per round-trip time and MUST NOT grow by more than SMSS bytes per RTT. One permitted formula is cwnd += SMSS*SMSS/cwnd per ACK for new data.

When the retransmission timer detects loss, ssthresh MUST be set to no more than max (FlightSize / 2, 2*SMSS), and cwnd MUST be set to no more than the loss window, which is one full-sized segment. The sender then uses slow start up to the new ssthresh.
sections.eli5: Slow start is like testing bath water: you begin with a little, and as long as it feels fine you keep adding more, quickly at first, then more gently. If you hit something too hot, you back off to about half and start again.

sections.title: Fast Retransmit and Fast Recovery
sections.content:
A receiver SHOULD send an immediate duplicate ACK when an out-of-order segment arrives. Duplicate ACKs can come from dropped segments, network reordering, or replication of ACKs or data. After 3 duplicate ACKs, the sender retransmits the apparently missing segment without waiting for the retransmission timer. This is fast retransmit.

Fast recovery then governs sending until a non-duplicate ACK arrives. Slow start is not used because duplicate ACKs show segments are still leaving the network, so the ACK clock is preserved. The steps are:

  • On the first and second duplicate ACKs, a TCP SHOULD send previously unsent data (Limited Transmit, RFC 3042) without changing cwnd.
  • On the third, set ssthresh to no more than max (FlightSize / 2, 2*SMSS).
  • Retransmit the lost segment and set cwnd to ssthresh plus 3*SMSS.
  • For each further duplicate ACK, increase cwnd by SMSS.
  • Send new data if cwnd and the receiver window allow.
  • When an ACK for new data arrives, set cwnd to ssthresh, called deflating the window.

The RFC notes this does not recover efficiently from multiple losses in a single flight of packets.
sections.eli5: If a friend keeps telling you the same page number over and over, you guess that one page went missing and resend it right away, without waiting for a long timeout.

sections.title: Idle Restarts, ACKs and Loss Recovery
sections.content:
Idle connections. After a long idle time the ACK clock has drained, so TCP could blast a window-sized burst. TCP SHOULD set cwnd to no more than the restart window, defined as RW = min(IW,cwnd), before sending if it has not sent data for longer than the retransmission timeout.

Acknowledgments. The delayed ACK algorithm of RFC 1122 SHOULD be used. An ACK SHOULD be generated for at least every second full-sized segment and MUST be generated within 500 ms of the arrival of the first unacknowledged packet. Out-of-order segments SHOULD be acknowledged immediately, and so SHOULD segments that fill a gap. A receiver MUST NOT generate more than one ACK per incoming segment, other than to update the offered window.

Loss recovery. The RFC does not standardize improvements to fast retransmit and fast recovery but implicitly allows them if they follow its principles: ssthresh is cut on the first loss, sending is at most half the outstanding segments per RTT until repair, and then cwnd is at most ssthresh. It RECOMMENDS an advanced loss recovery algorithm such as those in RFC 3782 and RFC 3517.
sections.eli5: If you have not talked for a while, you should not shout at full volume right away. And when you get a message, you should answer promptly, but not twice for the same message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the algorithms make TCP slow down when it sees timeouts or duplicate ACKs, an attacker can hurt a connection by causing data or ACKs to be lost, or by forging excessive duplicate ACKs.

The opposite attack is worse: forging excessive duplicate ACKs or ACKs for new data can make endpoints respond more aggressively, and the RFC says this could drive part of the network into congestion collapse. In response to the ACK division attack, the RFC RECOMMENDS increasing cwnd by the number of bytes newly acknowledged rather than by a fixed amount per ACK. A TCP MAY also limit how often cwnd is inflated during loss recovery to the number of outstanding segments.

The Internet relies to a considerable degree on correct implementation of these algorithms to keep the network stable.
sections.eli5: Someone could lie to a sender and trick it into going too slow or too fast. Counting what was really delivered, rather than trusting each message, makes the trick harder.

sections.title: What Changed From RFC 2581
sections.content:
RFC 5681 changes several points relative to RFC 2581:

  • A specific definition of duplicate acknowledgment was added.
  • What to do with duplicate ACKs after the retransmission timer fires is explicitly left unspecified.
  • The initial window rules now allow the larger initial windows of RFC 3390, with steps for an MSS found too large by Path MTU Discovery.
  • The initial ssthresh SHOULD now be arbitrarily high, where it was previously MAY.
  • Appropriate Byte Counting (RFC 3465) is recommended, and so is Limited Transmit.
  • The restart window changed to min(IW,cwnd) from IW.
  • Implementors are now recommended to implement an advanced loss recovery algorithm.
sections.eli5: This version is the old rule book with the confusing parts fixed, a few safer defaults and some newer tricks added.

data.title: Window update formulas
data.code:
slow start (per ACK of new data):
  cwnd += min (N, SMSS)                (2)

congestion avoidance (alternative, per ACK):
  cwnd += SMSS*SMSS/cwnd               (3)

on retransmission timeout / third duplicate ACK:
  ssthresh = max (FlightSize / 2, 2*SMSS)   (4)

items.title: Slow start
items.text: Used when cwnd is below ssthresh; grows cwnd by at most SMSS per ACK of new data.

items.title: Congestion avoidance
items.text: Used when cwnd is above ssthresh; grows by about one segment per RTT.

items.title: Fast retransmit
items.text: Resends the missing segment after 3 duplicate ACKs.

items.title: Fast recovery
items.text: Keeps sending new data at a reduced cwnd until an ACK for new data arrives.
